newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-FABEL, TOMS LEAD QUAD CITY CLASSIC AFTER THREE ROUNDS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-FABEL, TOMS LEAD QUAD CITY CLASSIC AFTER THREE ROUNDS.

text.p: Brad Fabel and David Toms shared the lead after the third round of the $1.35 million Quad-City Classic Saturday, but there were plenty of golfers on their heels heading into the final 18 holes.

Fabel, a PGA Tour veteran and perrennial Quad City threat, fired his way to the top from the middle of the pack by making birdies on five of his first seven backside holes en route to a five-under-par 65 and a three-day total of 10-under 200.

Toms, a fifth-year Tour pro making his debut at Oakwood Country Club, started the day in the final twosome and was the only member of the lead pack to gain some ground. His three-under 67 included a birdie at the 18th hole.
Four players -- Russ Cochran, Robert Gamez, Frank Lickliter and Brandel Chamblee -- were a shot out of the lead. Another five including second-round leader Keith Fergus were just two behind.

Another 50 players were within seven shots of the lead. Lickliter opened Saturday's action seven shots behind, and vaulted into Sunday's final trio after Saturday's tourney-low round of seven-under 63.
"There are a lot of guys who have a chance to win," said Fabel, who mined coal before stepping out onto the Tour in 1981. "I wouldn't be surprised if I'm off the leaderboard by the time I tee off."

Fergus, a three-time winner in the early 1980s, is making a PGA Tour comeback after taking seven years off to coach the University of Houston golf team. He said bunched Sunday leaderboards have become a fact of life on Tour since he joined the circuit in 1977.
"Back then, though, not everyone within range was a certifiable threat. Now, virtually to a man, they are.
"More guys think they can win," he said. "And more guys can win. If you stumble a little bit, somebody will run right by you."
Fabel had the best kick on Saturday thanks to the roar of a motorcycle, even though he missed a three-foot birdie putt at 18 that would have matched Fuzzy Zoeller's backside nine-hole record of 28.
"On my backswing on the putt," he said, "I heard someone crank up a Harley. I love Harleys so I thought, oh, a friend."
